Can you please introduce yourself?: Structure this in three parts under 90 seconds: a one-line professional summary (years of experience, core specialization), a brief walk through career progression highlighting the roles and platforms most relevant to this job, and a closing line connecting your background to why this specific opportunity interests you - avoid reciting your full resume chronologically.
What kind of tasks/activities do you do: Describe a realistic mix: a portion on production support/on-call, a portion on planned platform work (CI/CD pipeline changes, Helm chart updates, Terraform changes), and a portion on collaboration (reviewing deployment PRs, responding to application teams' infra requests). Naming the actual proportions and one concrete recent example (a pipeline you improved, an incident you resolved) reads as more credible than a generic list of tools.
Can you explain your CI/CD flow?: Walk it end to end in order: a developer commits/opens a PR, CI runs (build, unit tests, static analysis, security/image scanning), a container image is built and pushed to a registry tagged with the commit SHA, the new tag is updated in the Helm chart/values file, and CD takes over - either a direct Helm deploy from the pipeline, or a GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux) picking up the updated manifests and reconciling the cluster. Naming the actual tools at each stage (Jenkins/GitHub Actions, Docker, Artifact Registry/ECR, Helm, ArgoCD) grounds this in a specific, credible pipeline rather than a generic description.
Can you explain the CI/CD flow specifica: Narrow the general CI/CD answer to just the deployment half: once an image is built and pushed, the deployment flow updates the image reference in the Helm chart (a values.yaml or a templated tag), commits that change to the GitOps-tracked manifests repo, and a GitOps controller (or a direct `helm upgrade` step in the pipeline) reconciles the target cluster to match - with promotion between environments (dev to staging to prod) gated by either automatic promotion on successful health checks or a manual approval step for production.
How does the deployment stage work?: The deployment stage takes a specific, already-built and already-scanned image tag and applies it to the target environment - either imperatively (the pipeline runs `helm upgrade --install` or `kubectl apply` directly against the cluster) or declaratively via GitOps (the pipeline only updates a manifest/values file in Git, and a separate controller like ArgoCD detects that change and applies it). Health checks (readiness probes, a post-deploy smoke test) gate whether the deployment is considered successful, with automatic rollback if they fail.
How does your multi-stage deployment flo: Describe promotion as a sequence of gates, not a single push everywhere at once: an image built once and promoted unchanged through dev (auto-deployed on every merge), staging/QA (auto-deployed, with integration tests run against it), and production (gated behind a manual approval or automated canary analysis) - the same immutable image/tag moves through environments via updated Helm values or Kustomize overlays per environment, rather than being rebuilt per environment, which keeps what's tested in staging identical to what reaches production.
What tools do you use for application bu: List with the specific role each plays - source control (GitHub/GitLab), CI orchestration (Jenkins/GitHub Actions), containerization (Docker), image registry (Artifact Registry/ECR), templating (Helm), and deployment (ArgoCD for GitOps, or direct kubectl/Helm from the pipeline) - depth on how they connect together matters more than the tool list itself.
Once the Docker image tag is updated in: It depends on the deployment model: in a GitOps setup, committing the updated tag to the Git-tracked values file is what triggers it - ArgoCD (or Flux) is continuously polling or webhook-notified of the Git change, detects the manifests now differ from the live cluster state, and syncs (auto-sync) or waits for a manual sync click. In a non-GitOps pipeline, the trigger is simply the pipeline's own deploy stage running `helm upgrade` directly against the cluster right after the tag is updated - there's no separate detection step since the pipeline itself performs the apply.
What is Jenkins's role, Helm's role, and: Jenkins orchestrates the pipeline - triggering on commits, running build/test/scan stages, and either calling Helm directly or committing the updated manifest to a GitOps repo. Helm is the templating and packaging layer - it takes a chart (parameterized Kubernetes YAML) plus environment-specific values and renders the final manifests, and tracks release history for rollback. Kubernetes is the actual runtime - it takes the rendered manifests (from Helm or ArgoCD) and reconciles the cluster's real state (creating/updating Pods, Services, etc.) to match them. Each layer has a distinct, non-overlapping responsibility: orchestration, templating, and runtime.
If someone makes a manual change directl: In a GitOps-managed cluster, this is treated as drift to be corrected, not preserved - the GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux) continuously reconciles live state back to match Git, so a manual `kubectl edit` gets silently reverted on the next sync if self-heal is enabled. The correct process for an intentional emergency change is to make the same change in the Git-tracked manifest and let the controller apply it (or temporarily pause auto-sync, apply the fix, then immediately follow up with a matching Git commit) - never leave a manual change unsynced with Git, since it will eventually be reverted or confuse the next person investigating cluster state.
How does GitOps/Argo CD detect configura: ArgoCD continuously (or on a polling interval) compares the live state of resources in the cluster against the desired state declared in the Git repository it's tracking for that Application - any field-level difference is reported as 'OutOfSync.' If `selfHeal` is enabled in the sync policy, ArgoCD automatically re-applies the Git-declared state to correct the drift; without it, the Application just shows OutOfSync until someone triggers a manual sync.
How do you get a notification when someo: Configure ArgoCD Notifications (the built-in notifications controller) with a trigger on the `on-sync-status-unknown`/`on-deployed` style events - specifically a trigger condition watching for an Application transitioning to OutOfSync - wired to a notification service (Slack, email, a webhook to PagerDuty/Opsgenie) so the moment drift is detected, the configured channel gets an alert, rather than someone having to notice it in the ArgoCD UI.
How do you identify who made the manual: Cross-reference the timestamp ArgoCD reported the resource going OutOfSync against Kubernetes/cloud provider audit logs (Cloud Audit Logs on GKE, or the Kubernetes API server's own audit log) filtered to that resource and time window - the audit log entry for the mutating request (a PATCH/UPDATE call) records the exact user or service account identity that made it, which ArgoCD's drift detection alone does not capture since it only reports what changed, not who changed it.
What information/components do you check: Filter by the affected resource (kind, name, namespace) and the approximate time window drift was detected, then look at the request's method/verb (PATCH, UPDATE, DELETE), the requesting identity (`user.username` or the service account), the source IP, and the response status - together these tell you exactly what was changed, by whom, from where, and whether the request actually succeeded.
What are the important audit-log details: The core fields to check on every audit log entry: the identity (`user.username`/service account, since this is who to follow up with), the verb/operation (create, update, patch, delete - what kind of change was made), the object reference (resource kind, name, namespace - exactly what was touched), and the timestamp (to correlate precisely with when drift or an incident was first observed) - a complete picture requires all four together, since any one alone is ambiguous (e.g. knowing 'someone deleted something' without knowing what or when isn't actionable).
How do you set up Argo CD for applicatio: Install ArgoCD into the cluster (via its official manifests or the Helm chart), then define an Application resource pointing at a Git repository/path containing the application's manifests (raw YAML, Kustomize, or a Helm chart) and the target cluster/namespace to deploy into - configure the sync policy (manual or automated, with or without self-heal and pruning), and ArgoCD takes it from there, continuously reconciling the target cluster to match that Git source.
What components/configurations are requi: At minimum: the ArgoCD core components themselves (API server, repo server, application controller) installed in the cluster; an Application (or ApplicationSet for many services) CRD defining the source repo/path and destination cluster/namespace; RBAC/service accounts scoping what ArgoCD itself and its users are allowed to manage; Git repository credentials so ArgoCD can read (and for some workflows, write) the manifests repo; and, for production use, notification configuration and, if managing multiple clusters, registered cluster credentials.
How do you configure service accounts, R: Service accounts/RBAC: ArgoCD's own service accounts are scoped via Kubernetes RBAC to only the namespaces/resources it needs to manage per Application, and ArgoCD's internal RBAC (its `argocd-rbac-cm` ConfigMap) controls which human users/groups can view or sync which Applications/Projects. Secrets: application-level secrets are kept out of the Git repo entirely, synced instead via Sealed Secrets or the External Secrets Operator referencing a real secrets manager. Git repository access: a deploy key, HTTPS token, or GitHub App credential is registered in ArgoCD's repository settings (stored as a Kubernetes Secret) so it can clone/read the manifests repo. Webhooks: a webhook from the Git provider to ArgoCD's API server enables near-instant sync detection instead of relying only on the polling interval. Notifications: the ArgoCD Notifications controller is configured with trigger conditions (sync status changes, health degradation) and notification service credentials (Slack webhook URL, SMTP, PagerDuty API key) to route alerts to the right channel.
Design a deployment order using ArgoCD s: Annotate the migration Job with `argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync` (and a wave number if other PreSync work must run before it) so it runs and must complete before the main Sync phase applies the Deployment; annotate a smoke-test Job with `PostSync` so it only runs after the new Pods are deployed and healthy. If the PreSync hook fails, ArgoCD marks the sync operation as Failed and does not proceed to apply the main manifests at all - the Deployment is never touched, which is exactly the safety property you want (no point rolling out new Pods against a database that failed its migration). The failure is visible in the Application's sync status and history, and by default ArgoCD does not auto-retry a failed hook unless a retry strategy is explicitly configured.
You need to deploy the same application: Use the ApplicationSet cluster generator, which auto-discovers every cluster registered with ArgoCD (or filtered by label) and templates one Application per cluster, injecting per-cluster values (cluster name, custom labels/annotations you've set on the cluster secret) into each generated Application's parameters - so per-cluster config differences are handled via generator template variables rather than 50 hand-maintained Application manifests. To prevent one bad cluster from blocking the others, configure the ApplicationSet's rollout strategy (`strategy: RollingSync`) with progressive batches (a few clusters at a time) rather than all-at-once, so a failure is caught and halts further batches before affecting all 50 - critically, each generated Application is independent, so a sync failure on one cluster's Application does not block or roll back the Applications already successfully synced on other clusters.
How would you configure ArgoCD sync wind: Define a `SyncWindow` on the relevant AppProject with `kind: deny`, a schedule matching the freeze period (cron syntax), and scoped to the specific Applications/clusters under freeze - this blocks automatic (and by default manual) syncs during that window. To still allow emergency manual syncs during the freeze, set `manualSync: true` on that deny window, which permits an explicit manual sync to bypass the block while automatic syncs (triggered by a Git change or the polling loop) remain blocked - giving you a hard freeze against accidental/automatic deploys while preserving a deliberate, explicit escape hatch for genuine emergencies.
Design a hub-and-spoke ArgoCD architectu: One central ArgoCD instance registers all 20 remote clusters' credentials (via `argocd cluster add` or cluster Secrets) and manages Applications targeting each as a destination - the hub cluster runs the ArgoCD control plane; the spoke clusters just receive applied manifests via the Kubernetes API, with no ArgoCD components running on them. If the hub goes down: existing workloads on all 20 spoke clusters keep running completely unaffected, since they don't depend on ArgoCD at runtime - but no new syncs can happen anywhere, drift detection stops, and any in-flight sync at the moment of failure may be left partially applied. This is exactly why the hub cluster itself needs its own high-availability design (multiple replicas of ArgoCD's components, its own backup/DR plan) - it becomes a single point of failure for deployment capability across the entire fleet, even though it's not a single point of failure for already-running application traffic.
ArgoCD shows a custom CRD-backed Applica: ArgoCD's built-in health check logic only understands well-known resource types (Deployments, StatefulSets, Services, Ingress) - a custom CRD has no built-in health assessment, so ArgoCD defaults to either 'Healthy' immediately (wrong if the CRD's controller needs time to reconcile) or 'Progressing' indefinitely if the CRD's status conditions don't match any pattern ArgoCD recognizes. Fix by defining a custom health check in Lua for that specific CRD (in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap under `resource.customizations.health`), inspecting that CRD's actual `.status` fields (e.g. a `conditions` array with a `Ready` type) to return `Healthy`/`Progressing`/`Degraded` correctly based on what the CRD's own controller actually reports.
An HPA-managed Deployment's replica coun: This is the classic conflict between two controllers both wanting to own the same field: Git declares a fixed `replicas` count, but HPA is actively adjusting it based on load, so ArgoCD sees the live replica count differ from Git's declared count and reports drift. Fix with a targeted `ignoreDifferences` rule on that Application scoped specifically to `spec.replicas` on that Deployment (via `jsonPointers` or `jqPathExpressions`) - this tells ArgoCD to stop comparing that one field while still fully enforcing and self-healing every other field, which is the correct scoped fix versus disabling self-heal for the whole Application (which would also stop protecting against genuine unwanted drift on everything else).
Your ArgoCD control-plane cluster is des: First confirm the actual application workloads on the spoke/target clusters are unaffected (per the earlier point, they run independently of ArgoCD at runtime) - there's no immediate outage to firefight, which removes time pressure. Recovery: provision a new cluster (or reuse a recovered one) for the ArgoCD control plane, reinstall ArgoCD, re-register each target cluster's credentials, and re-create the Application/ApplicationSet/AppProject resources - if these were themselves managed via an 'app of apps' pattern stored in Git (the recommended practice specifically for this scenario), a single `kubectl apply` of the root Application bootstraps the entire fleet of Applications back automatically, rather than manually recreating dozens of Application manifests by hand. This is exactly why ArgoCD's own configuration should itself be GitOps-managed, not just the applications it deploys.
Design a process to rotate a database cr: Rotate the actual secret value in the underlying secrets manager (Secret Manager/Vault) first, then let External Secrets Operator's existing refresh interval pick up the new value and update the Kubernetes Secret in place - if the consuming Pods mount the Secret as a volume, most applications will see the updated file without a restart (kubelet propagates volume-mounted Secret updates, typically within a minute, though the application itself must re-read the file rather than caching it at startup). For applications that only read the credential as an environment variable at process start (which never reflects a later Secret update), those specific Deployments genuinely do need a rolling restart to pick up the new value - but this is scoped to only the apps using the env-var pattern, not blanket-redeploying all 40 via a Git commit, which would be unnecessary churn for the volume-mount-based ones.
A PostSync hook Job fails intermittently: A failed PostSync hook marks the overall sync operation as Failed/Degraded even though the main application manifests were already successfully applied in the Sync phase before it - which can be confusing since the actual application is running fine but ArgoCD shows the deploy as failed. Design the hook Job with Kubernetes-native retries (`backoffLimit` on the Job spec) so transient flakiness is absorbed at the Job level before ArgoCD ever sees a failure, make the hook itself idempotent (safe to run multiple times with the same effect, e.g. a smoke test that only reads/checks rather than mutates), and use the `PostSync` hook's own `hook-delete-policy` (e.g. `BeforeHookCreation`) so a retried sync doesn't collide with a leftover Job object from the previous attempt.
You're evaluating ArgoCD vs Flux for an: ArgoCD's built-in multi-tenancy (Projects, its own RBAC and SSO-integrated UI) and strong visual UI make it a better fit when many teams need self-service visibility and permission boundaries without heavy custom tooling - a real advantage at 15-team scale. Flux's more Kubernetes-native, API-driven, no-UI-by-default design (everything as CRDs, no separate web UI to secure/scale) fits teams that prefer pure GitOps-as-code and want tighter integration with existing Kubernetes tooling/observability rather than a distinct product UI. At 300+ microservices, the deciding factors in practice are usually: whether teams need ArgoCD's UI-driven self-service (favors ArgoCD) versus a lighter-weight, more composable, UI-optional footprint (favors Flux), and which the platform team already has deeper operational experience with, since both are capable of the same core reconciliation guarantees at this scale.
A developer with 'sync' permission on on: Audit the AppProject's `destinations` field first - if it's scoped too broadly (a wildcard cluster/namespace rather than the specific ones that team owns), any Application created under that Project can target any destination matching the wildcard, regardless of the RBAC policy governing sync permissions, since destination scoping and sync-action RBAC are two separate controls that must both be tightened. Fix by restricting the Project's `destinations` list to only the specific clusters/namespaces that team should ever deploy to, and separately review the `argocd-rbac-cm` policy rules granting sync permission to confirm they're scoped to `project:<team-project>` rather than a broader or default policy that inadvertently grants cross-project access.
Your root 'app of apps' Application itse: Deleting the root Application (by default) does not cascade-delete the child Applications it manages or their underlying Kubernetes resources - ArgoCD's default deletion behavior only removes the Application resource itself unless cascade deletion was explicitly configured/confirmed, so running workloads typically keep running untouched. What breaks is future reconciliation of that app-of-apps tree - no new child Applications will be created and existing ones won't be updated via this path until the root is restored. Recovery is straightforward specifically because app-of-apps is meant to be idempotent and Git-sourced: re-apply the root Application manifest (from Git, where it should already be version-controlled) and ArgoCD recreates the entire child Application tree and resumes normal reconciliation, with no need to manually recreate anything by hand.
Design an automated canary using Argo Ro: Use an Argo Rollouts `canary` strategy with weighted steps (e.g. 5% traffic, pause with an `AnalysisRun`, then increase) integrated with a service mesh (Istio VirtualService weights) for the actual traffic split. The `AnalysisTemplate` queries Prometheus for the canary's error rate and p99 latency over a short, tight interval (e.g. every 15-30 seconds) against a defined failure threshold, with `failureLimit` set low (e.g. 1-2 consecutive failed checks) so a genuine regression is caught within 2-3 analysis intervals - comfortably inside a 2-minute window - at which point Argo Rollouts automatically aborts the rollout and shifts all traffic back to the stable version without any human intervention.
Your GitOps manifests repo has grown to: The repo-server has to clone/fetch and render (via Helm/Kustomize) the entire repo (or the relevant path) on each refresh, so a huge monorepo with thousands of files makes every render cycle slower even for Applications only watching a small subdirectory - check repo-server CPU/memory and its manifest generation latency metrics first to confirm this is actually the bottleneck rather than something else (network, Git host latency). Fix by scaling the repo-server horizontally (it supports multiple replicas), enabling manifest caching, narrowing each Application's configured path as tightly as possible so it doesn't need to evaluate irrelevant parts of the repo, and considering splitting the single giant monorepo into per-team repos if the org has genuinely outgrown a shared monorepo's practical scaling limits.
Two ArgoCD Applications with overlapping: Both Applications will repeatedly try to reconcile that resource to their own (potentially different) desired state, causing a visible fight - the resource's fields flip back and forth between what each Application declares, and both Applications may perpetually show as OutOfSync or repeatedly re-sync against each other's changes. Prevent this at the design level with a strict rule that every Kubernetes resource is declared in exactly one place in Git, owned by exactly one Application - use distinct, non-overlapping paths/labels per Application, and treat any accidental overlap discovered later as an immediate cleanup task (removing the duplicate declaration from one of the two sources) rather than something to work around with tooling, since no ArgoCD setting resolves a fundamental double-ownership conflict cleanly.
